title: Dynamic Language Runtimes — V8 & CPython
summary: How runtimes make dynamically-typed languages fast, or don't. V8's hidden classes turn objects into something JIT-friendly; CPython mostly skips that fight entirely, and pays for it with the GIL.

slides.markdown:
Everything so far — the JVM, the CLR — is a statically-typed source language on a managed runtime. Dynamically-typed languages face a harder problem: the type of `x` in `x.foo` can change between calls, so the runtime can't assume a fixed memory layout the way a statically-typed compiler can.

**V8** (JavaScript's runtime in Chrome and Node.js) attacks this head-on with hidden classes and aggressive JIT speculation. **CPython** (the reference Python runtime) mostly doesn't — it stays a straightforward bytecode interpreter, which is a large part of why "Python is slow" is a more defensible claim than "Java is slow."

This topic covers both, and ends on the GIL — the single most commonly-asked CPython concurrency question in interviews.

In Java, `obj.field` compiles to a fixed-offset memory read, because the compiler statically knows `obj`'s type and therefore exactly where `field` lives in memory. In JavaScript or Python, the equivalent `obj.field` access has to handle "what if this particular object doesn't have `field`, or has it at a different position, or `obj`'s type changed since the last time this line ran."

Every property access, method call, and arithmetic operation in a dynamically-typed language pays this tax: some amount of runtime lookup work a statically-typed language's compiler eliminated ahead of time. The two runtimes in this topic represent two different answers to "how much can we claw back."

slides.subTitle: Giving dynamic objects a static-like layout
slides.markdown:
V8's answer: even though JavaScript objects are dynamically typed, most objects created by the same piece of code end up with the same set of properties in the same order. V8 detects this and assigns them a shared **hidden class** (also called a "shape" or "map") — an internal, invisible-to-JS-code descriptor of "which properties, at which offsets."

Two objects `{x: 1, y: 2}` created the same way get the same hidden class, so accessing `.x` on either one becomes a fixed-offset read — exactly the trick a statically-typed compiler gets for free, recovered dynamically by observing the actual shapes objects take at runtime.

Adding a property in a different order (`{y: 2, x: 1}` vs `{x: 1, y: 2}`) or adding properties dynamically after construction can create a *different* hidden class, which is where this optimization quietly breaks.

slides.markdown:
`just-in-time-compilation` introduced inline caches generically; V8 is where they were popularized for dynamic languages. A property-access call site remembers the last hidden class it saw. Next time through, V8 checks "is this object the same hidden class as last time?" — if yes, it skips straight to the cached offset instead of a full property lookup.

This is the same monomorphic → polymorphic → megamorphic ladder from `just-in-time-compilation`: a call site that only ever sees one hidden class stays fast (monomorphic inline cache); one that sees a handful still benefits from a checked cache (polymorphic); one that sees many different shapes falls back to slow generic lookup (megamorphic) — which is exactly why constructing objects inconsistently (sometimes with a property, sometimes without) is a real, measurable V8 performance anti-pattern, not superstition.

CPython compiles Python source to bytecode (viewable via the `dis` module) and runs it with a straightforward interpreter loop — fetch instruction, dispatch on opcode, execute, repeat. No hidden classes, no speculative inline caching of the V8 kind, and — until very recent CPython versions began adding a limited JIT — no JIT compilation of hot code to native instructions at all.

Every Python object is a heap-allocated `PyObject` with reference counting built into its header, and attribute access on most objects goes through a dictionary lookup on `__dict__` rather than a fixed offset. This is deliberately simple and highly compatible (CPython is the reference implementation every Python library targets), at a real, structural performance cost relative to V8's approach.

slides.subTitle: One lock, one running thread at a time
slides.markdown:
The **Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)** is a single lock that CPython holds while executing Python bytecode. Only one thread can hold it at a time, so even on an 8-core machine, only one thread is ever executing Python bytecode at any given instant — other threads wait.

Why CPython has this at all: it makes reference counting (the mechanism behind Python's memory management) simple and fast to implement without needing atomic operations on every single increment/decrement, and it made the original CPython implementation dramatically simpler to get right. The GIL is released periodically (every N bytecode instructions, or explicitly around blocking I/O calls) so threads *do* get to interleave — just never run Python bytecode truly in parallel.

slides.sectionTitle: What the GIL means for CPU-bound code
slides.markdown:
The pitfall this produces constantly: adding `threading` to CPU-bound Python code expecting a speedup, and getting none — sometimes even a slowdown from lock contention overhead.

```python
import threading

def cpu_heavy():
    total = 0
    for i in range(50_000_000):
        total += i * i
    return total

# Running this on 4 threads does NOT run 4x faster.
# The GIL means only one thread executes Python bytecode
# at a time — the threads take turns, not run in parallel.
threads = [threading.Thread(target=cpu_heavy) for _ in range(4)]
```

The fix isn't "use fewer threads" — it's picking the right concurrency tool for CPU-bound work: `multiprocessing` (separate processes, each with its own GIL and interpreter, genuine parallelism at the cost of IPC overhead) or dropping into a C extension / NumPy vectorized call that releases the GIL while it runs. `threading` in CPython is for *I/O-bound* concurrency (`async-await-and-cooperative-concurrency` covers the alternative model), not CPU parallelism.

slides.sectionTitle: Why I/O-bound threading still works fine
slides.markdown:
The GIL is specifically about *Python bytecode* execution, not about threads existing at all — which is why threading remains genuinely useful in CPython for I/O-bound work.

When a thread makes a blocking call (reading a socket, waiting on a file), CPython releases the GIL for the duration of that wait, letting another thread run Python code while the first one is blocked on the OS. Ten threads each waiting on a slow network call genuinely overlap their *waiting* time, even though they can never overlap their Python-bytecode-*executing* time.

This is the practical resolution to "but I've seen threading speed things up in Python" — it did, because the workload was I/O-bound, where the GIL is a non-issue, not CPU-bound, where it's the whole story.

slides.sectionTitle: V8's JIT-heavy approach vs CPython's interpreter-first approach
slides.markdown:
| | V8 (JavaScript) | CPython |
|---|---|---|
| Object layout | Hidden classes recover a static-like shape | Dictionary-backed `__dict__`, no shape inference |
| Hot-path strategy | Multi-tier JIT (Ignition interpreter -> Sparkplug -> Maglev -> TurboFan) | Mostly interpreter-only historically; a limited JIT is new and narrow in scope |
| Call-site optimization | Inline caches, monomorphic/polymorphic/megamorphic | None equivalent by default |
| Multi-core parallelism (single process) | Not limited by an equivalent global lock | Limited by the GIL for CPU-bound Python bytecode |

The practical consequence: V8-run JavaScript on a hot loop can approach statically-typed-language speed; CPython on the equivalent loop generally can't, without dropping into C-backed libraries (NumPy, and similar) that skip the interpreter loop entirely for the actual numeric work.

slides.sectionTitle: PyPy and the road not taken
slides.markdown:
CPython's design isn't the only possible answer for Python — **PyPy**, an alternative Python implementation, has a JIT and routinely runs CPU-bound Python code several times faster than CPython on long-running workloads, using techniques much closer to V8's.

PyPy isn't the default because C-extension compatibility (NumPy, pandas, and most of the scientific/ML ecosystem are written against CPython's specific C API) is imperfect on PyPy, and most production Python code depends on at least one such extension. This is the real reason "Python is slow" survives as a claim about *CPython specifically* — the language itself doesn't force an interpreter-only design, the dominant implementation's ecosystem commitments do.

"Why doesn't multithreading speed up this CPU-bound Python function?" has a complete answer in three parts:

1. **Name the mechanism.** The GIL allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, regardless of core count.
2. **Distinguish the workload.** It matters whether the bottleneck is CPU (bytecode execution itself) or I/O (waiting on something external) — the GIL only blocks the former.
3. **Name the actual fix.** `multiprocessing` for genuine parallelism, or push the hot loop into a C extension / vectorized library that releases the GIL.

Contrast this with V8: JavaScript doesn't have an equivalent GIL constraint for its own single-threaded model, but Node.js's own concurrency story (`async-await-and-cooperative-concurrency`) is single-threaded by design for a different reason — one event loop, not a lock protecting reference counts.
